researched_by: the Park Authority's own visitor guidance, byelaw pages and Local Development Plan evidence base, plus operator websites for each stopover and park4night/campercontact for coordinates
policy_summary:
The largest national park in the UK, and the clearest counter-example to Loch Lomond. There are NO camping management byelaws in the Cairngorms and never have been. Nothing here makes it an offence to sleep in a vehicle anywhere in the park's 4,528 square kilometres. The Authority's published line is permissive and unusually explicit: 'roadside laybys may be used for overnight parking, but not camping' - stay inside the van, no awnings, tables, chairs or cooking outside - while 'off-road parking (including car parks) overnight requires the permission of the landowner'.

The Cairngorms does have byelaws, and this is where people get confused. The Cairngorms National Park Fire Management Byelaw was approved by Scottish Ministers on 25 September 2025 and first bit on 1 April 2026. From 1 April to 30 September each year it bans fires, disposable and charcoal barbecues, fire pits and wood or coal burning stoves across the ENTIRE park, with a fine of up to GBP500, enforced by Police Scotland and CNPA rangers. Gas and liquid-fuel stoves and gas barbecues are still permitted, so a van cooking on gas is fine. It is a fire byelaw, not a camping byelaw, and it does not touch where you may park or sleep.

The Authority runs no aires and owns essentially no car parks. What it does instead is signpost a network of small private and community stopovers - Cairngorm Mountain's 45-pitch site at Coire na Ciste, the Kingussie aire at Croila Croft, Glenshee Ski Centre, Castle Roy at Nethy Bridge, Ar-Dachaigh Croft at Carrbridge, Tomintoul Bowling Club, and Balmoral's car park at Crathie. Prices run from a donation to GBP20. Provision in this park is landowner policy, not parking orders.

Direction of travel is towards more provision, slowly. The Local Development Plan evidence base records motorhome use rising from 8% to 10% of overnight visitors between 2019-20 and 2024-25, and informal motorhome parking more than doubling from 3% to 7%, with Dalwhinnie, Grantown-on-Spey, Laggan, Newtonmore, Carrbridge and Nethy Bridge all asking for serviced sites. A 'network of motorhome facilities' sits on the Sustainable Tourism Infrastructure list as a MEDIUM priority. Nothing has been built at scale.
notes:
THE ABSENCE IS THE FINDING. Loch Lomond and The Trossachs made sleeping in a vehicle inside a Camping Management Zone a criminal offence in 2017. The Cairngorms, four times the size and with the same pressures, has never done it. Successive Chief Executives have declined to rule byelaws out permanently, and Parkswatch Scotland's 2020 analysis notes the Authority repeatedly cites its byelaw-making powers rather than committing to build service points - but as of July 2026 the powers remain unused for camping. If you want to know what Scotland looks like without camping byelaws, this is it.

SECOND POINT, AND IT IS THE ONE PEOPLE GET WRONG. The permissiveness here is not a right. The Authority's own informal camping guidance states flatly that 'overnight stays in campervans or motorhomes is not covered by access rights' - the Land Reform (Scotland) Act 2003 and the Scottish Outdoor Access Code cover people on foot, not motor vehicles. The guidance goes further and kills the usual folk defence: section 34 of the Road Traffic Act 1988 lets you drive up to 15 yards off a road solely to park, but 'this exception does not confer any right to park the vehicle on the land', so parking off-road without permission is trespass. A tent 20 metres from the road is exercising a statutory right. A van in the same spot is not. The lay-by is the safe line here, exactly as it is at Loch Lomond, but for a different reason: there it is a byelaw exemption, here it is the boundary of the public road.

THIRD, THE AUTHORITY IS NOT THE ROADS AUTHORITY. CNPA has no traffic regulation powers. Every road, lay-by and council car park inside the boundary belongs to Highland, Aberdeenshire, Moray, Angus or Perth and Kinross. That split produced the sharpest episode in this park's recent history: Highland Council consulted in autumn 2023 on year-round charging and a ban on stays over 24 hours at Glenmore and Loch Morlich, the busiest honeypot in the park; Mountaineering Scotland, Cairngorm Runners and Nethy Bridge Community Council objected; and in February 2024 the council dropped the overnight ban and cut charging back to 1 March - 31 October. The national park authority had no formal role in a decision about the most visited place in its own park.

FOURTH, AND WORTH RECORDING FOR THE REGISTER. None of the twelve car parks in The Highland Council's GBP40 campervan pass scheme lie inside the Cairngorms - they are all Wester Ross, Caithness, Sutherland, Inverness and Nairn. Aberdeenshire runs no aire scheme on Deeside. So the Badenoch and Strathspey and Deeside sides of the park get no local-authority overnight provision at all, and the entire supply is private and community-run. That is why a 45-pitch commercial site on a ski car park at 543 metres is the largest legal stopover in Britain's biggest national park.

Fifth, a practical note on facilities. Waste disposal for non-residents is available for a charge at Oakwood and Dalraddy near Aviemore, Grantown on Spey Caravan Park, Blair Castle, Braemar Caravan Park and the Muir of Dinnet NNR car park. Grantown is the only one that is not a holiday park.

OWN-PROVISION SWEEP, 27 July 2026 - NIL RETURN. Country parks, Authority-run campsites, caravan sites, aires and Authority-owned car parks with overnight permission were all checked. THE CAIRNGORMS NATIONAL PARK AUTHORITY OWNS AND RUNS NO OVERNIGHT PROVISION OF ANY KIND.

The cleanest proof is the Authority's own visitor centres page. It lists twenty visitor and information centres across the park and operates NOT ONE of them - every entry belongs to Forestry and Land Scotland, Balmoral, RSPB, Rothiemurchus, Glen Tanar, Glenlivet, Cairngorm Mountain, a community group or a business. An authority that owned staffed visitor infrastructure would appear on its own list. It does not, which is consistent with the third point above: CNPA has no traffic regulation powers and very little land, so every site in this file is somebody else's.

That makes the Cairngorms the mirror image of Loch Lomond and The Trossachs, which not only made byelaws but built and now runs four campsites and sells motorhome permits. Same country, same problem, two national park authorities, and only one of them is in the accommodation business.

Whether CNPA has GRANT-FUNDED facilities it does not own - Rural Tourism Infrastructure Fund waste points, Cairngorms 2030 works - could not be established and is logged as an open question. A grant is not provision, but it would tell you where the facilities came from.
open_questions: The Cairngorm Mountain stopover price: the operator's own page says GBP17.50, park4night reports GBP20 and searchforsites GBP15. GBP17.50 recorded on the operator's authority; check at booking.
Does the Cairngorm site really open free of charge outside the 1 May - 31 Oct season when the gate is up, as park4night reviewers claim? The operator publishes a season, not a winter policy.
Tomintoul Bowling Club season: VisitCairngorms says year-round, campercontact says 26 March to 1 November. Unresolved.

Is there any live proposal for camping management byelaws in the Cairngorms? Nothing found for 2025-26, but the Authority has never formally ruled them out and the 2026 Loch Lomond byelaw review could shift the argument either way.
What has actually been delivered from the 'network of motorhome facilities' project in the Sustainable Tourism Infrastructure Plan? Only the Glenshee toilets and waste point are named as funded.
Whether any of the five constituent councils has an overnight-parking prohibition on a specific road or car park inside the park boundary. No TRO text was found; the Glenmore proposal was withdrawn.
Whether the estates (Mar Lodge/NTS, Balmoral, Glenfeshie, Rothiemurchus) publish overnight vehicle policies beyond the Crathie car park. Not found.

Has CNPA grant-funded motorhome waste or service points through the Rural Tourism Infrastructure Fund or Cairngorms 2030? A grant is not CNPA provision but would explain where the community-run facilities in this file came from. Not established.

The Authority's interactive map is said to show aire and waste-point pins but is JavaScript-driven and its data layer could not be read. Those pins are the only published list of van facilities in the park.

sites.name: Cairngorm Motorhome Stopover, Coire na Ciste
sites.search_hint: Cairngorm Motorhome Stopover, Coire na Ciste car park, ski road above Glenmore
sites.notes: The largest legal overnight stopover in the National Park by a distance - 45 pitches on the old lower ski car park at about 543m, ten miles from Aviemore and three from Glenmore. Run by Cairngorm Mountain (Scotland) Ltd, the publicly owned operator, not by the Park Authority. Gated with a code issued on booking. No toilets or showers on site; those are at the main Cairngorm Mountain base a few minutes' drive up the road. Very exposed to wind - park nose into it. what3words ///wakes.originals.glow.

sites.name: Kingussie Camping and Motorhome Aire, Croila Croft
sites.price_note: GBP10 for a hardstanding aire pitch, GBP15 for a grass pitch, GBP5 for water and waste with no overnight stay
facilities: council toilets and showers 400m at Ardvonie car park
sites.search_hint: Croila Croft motorhome aire, Railway Station Industrial Estate, Ruthven Road, Kingussie
sites.notes: The only thing in the National Park that calls itself an aire and behaves like one - eleven hardstanding overnight pitches plus five Motor Caravanners Club grass pitches, open year-round, 200m from two pubs and 400m from the shops. Run by Highland Horse Fun from the old railway station yard. Also sells a GBP5 service-only stop, which makes it the most useful waste point in Badenoch for someone not staying.

sites.name: Glenshee Ski Centre, Cairnwell
sites.price_note: GBP8 without electric hook-up, GBP15 with; GBP5 each for chemical and grey waste disposal
sites.search_hint: Glenshee Snowsports Centre, Cairnwell, Braemar AB35 5XU
sites.notes: On the Cairnwell pass at about 2,200 feet, on the SnowRoads scenic route and right on the Aberdeenshire / Perth and Kinross boundary inside the park. Six hook-up pitches plus space in the main car park without. The 24-hour toilets, showers and motorhome waste point were a funded project under the CNPA-backed Strategic Tourism Infrastructure Development Plan 2023-28 - one of the few motorhome facilities in this park that public money actually delivered. Departure 10am without hook-up; hook-up bookings arrive 5pm and leave 4.30pm the next day.

sites.name: Castle Roy, Nethy Bridge
sites.price_note: donation only - QR code and honesty boxes on site; users report GBP5-GBP10 suggested
prohibits: emptying grey water anywhere on site
black waste disposal in the village public toilets
sites.search_hint: Castle Roy car park, B970 Grantown Road, north of Nethy Bridge
sites.notes: Three motorhomes in the car park of a 13th century castle ruin, on a donation basis, run by the Castle Roy Trust as a fundraiser. No facilities at all, and the Trust is emphatic about grey water because there are animals on the ground. Nearest Elsan point is the Nethy Bridge community centre. Open all year unless there is an event on. Approach from Grantown or Boat of Garten - the direct route crosses a 3-tonne weight-restricted bridge. The clearest example in this park of provision arising from a community trust rather than any authority.

sites.name: Formal lay-bys throughout the National Park
sites.notes: EXPLICITLY PERMITTED BY THE PARK AUTHORITY. Its own visitor guidance says 'roadside laybys may be used for overnight parking, but not camping' and that 'a designated formal lay-by' may be used 'to rest, including overnight in a motorhome' as long as everything stays inside the vehicle - no awnings, tables, chairs or cooking outside. Obey posted parking conditions and pay any charge, and be prepared to move. This is guidance, not a legal right: the roads belong to Highland, Aberdeenshire, Moray, Angus and Perth and Kinross, any of whom could make a traffic regulation order tomorrow. But no such order was found anywhere inside the park boundary.

sites.name: The National Park as a whole - no camping management byelaws
sites.notes: THE HEADLINE FACT. Unlike Loch Lomond and The Trossachs, the Cairngorms has never made camping management byelaws. There is no zone anywhere in the park's 4,528 square kilometres where sleeping in a vehicle is an offence, no permit system, and no seasonal camping ban. The Authority's wild camping page confirms camping is permitted throughout if done responsibly; the only park-wide byelaw is about fire. The Authority has repeatedly declined to rule byelaws out permanently, so this is a settled practice rather than a guarantee.

sites.name: Off-road overnight parking, including car parks, without landowner permission
sites.notes: The Authority's guidance is blunt: 'off-road parking (including car parks) overnight requires the permission of the landowner', and 'if parking off-road overnight, you should have the permission of the landowner' - if you cannot tell who owns it, park elsewhere. Its informal camping guidance spells out why: 'overnight stays in campervans or motorhomes is not covered by access rights'. The Land Reform (Scotland) Act 2003 and the Scottish Outdoor Access Code do not extend to motor vehicles. The guidance also closes the usual loophole - section 34 of the Road Traffic Act 1988 permits driving up to 15 yards off a road solely to park, but 'this exception does not confer any right to park the vehicle on the land', so it is trespass without permission. A civil matter, not a fixed penalty, which is why enforcement in practice is a knock on the window.

sites.name: Cairngorms National Park Fire Management Byelaw 2025 - park-wide fire and barbecue ban
sites.notes: NOT A PARKING OR SLEEPING RESTRICTION - it restricts fire, and it is recorded here because it is the only byelaw in this park and is routinely confused with Loch Lomond's camping byelaws. Approved by Scottish Ministers on 25 September 2025, first in force 1 April 2026, running 1 April to 30 September each year across the WHOLE park. Bans open fires, disposable and charcoal barbecues, fire pits, fire bowls and wood or coal burning stoves. Exempt: gas and liquid fuel camping stoves, gas barbecues, meths and solid fuel block stoves, gardens including holiday lets, registered campsites subject to site rules, bothies with existing fireplaces, and fires with written landowner permission. Up to GBP500, enforced by Police Scotland and CNPA rangers - in 2025 rangers spoke to 6,643 people and removed 615 fire sites. For a van user the practical effect is simple: cook on gas, do not light anything.
